doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

chapter: Hurricane Katrina and New Orleans today
title: Uneven recovery in the Lower Ninth Ward and saying both things about New Orleans
summary: He describes a Lower Ninth Ward high school still in temporary buildings against the quickly rebuilt Vietnamese community. He says the city is both not back to normal and ready for visitors.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: might have moved back to New Orleans to help rebuild their own city. I mean there’s all sorts of things and dynamics of it that are not hard to understand, but at the same time it’s disconcerting to realize that our country, for all the greatness of our resources, on two fronts has not embraced our own culture as something that’s kind of collectively ours to share and be proud of. But we’re also not really looking at each other as being one community. And those are the kind of two disconcerting things that show a real disconnect and a lack of compassion in situations like this. I think that’s something on a global level I think there’s a disconnect there that’s sort of part of the same cancer that makes it possible for whole nations to be rather insensitive to one another’s situation or needs and a lack of understanding and empathy that at the end of the day, and we’re close to the end of the day in a way, this planet is sort of ours to share and one person having things and another person not having things is, there may be some justice in it economically but unless everybody’s bailing water out of the boat together it doesn’t matter how much you have when you go down. So yeah, ironically, Monk, you know it’s funny about New Orleans is when people, I don’t know what it is, if it’s something about me personally, but I’ve talked to other people that the same thing happens with them. There are many places in New Orleans that have not changed a bit since August 29, 2005. I did some work at a high school recently that didn’t have any, they barely had anything before the storm, now they’ve got even less. And this high school is in the lower ninth ward and they are still in temporary buildings next door to where their school is. And George Washington Carver has a beautiful energy, the students have a beautiful energy in spite of how little they’ve been given to work with and in spite of how blighted their portion of the community is. Whereas not very far away in another part of the ninth ward, the Vietnamese rebuilt their schools and houses so fast they attracted the international attention of BNP Paribas and Ricoh Copiers, Ricoh Office Supplies, and got sponsorship to kind of rebuild. So yeah, there’s some disparity in the way people chose to enter this phase of recovery. But it’s funny, when people were saying, “Hey, so things in New Orleans, they’re back to normal, right?” I find myself getting defensive, saying, “hell no, they’re not back to normal.” And I’ll tell them about this high school and I’ll tell them about areas and houses in my own neighborhood that are still abandoned. And by the same token, if someone says, “Yeah, I can’t go back to New Orleans, man, things probably are really still terrible down there.” I find myself being the opposite and saying, “No, we’re ready for you, come on down, come and take a visit and see for yourself.” And you can say both things about it simultaneously. You can say that yeah, four years later we’re still in business and there’s still a lot of great music to be heard and you can still go to second lines on a Sunday and the food and music culture is still more unique than anything you’re going to find anywhere else in the United States and you need to

experience it. And at the same time I can say yeah, this place is, we’re still fighting over how to rebuild the hospitals. We’re still fighting over how to rebuild schools. We’re still arguing about what we’re going to do have more significant levy protection for future floods and it’s a mess. You can say those things simultaneously. It’s all part of a whole.
